claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy is nanocrystalline and contains Al, Fe, and other elements.
The initial alloy has a near-equiatomic composition.
The initial alloy lacks an optimized pre-formed passive oxide layer.
Sintering near 1000 °C promotes surface enrichment in key elements.
Sintering near 1000 °C induces a dense, continuous, spinel-type surface oxide film.
Simultaneous wear-corrosion resistance is governed by the in situ oxide film.
The oxide film reduces exposed active-metal area and impedes corrosive ion transport as a diffusion barrier.
The oxide film is sufficiently hard and mechanically integral to delay removal during abrasive or sliding wear.
Microcracks in the oxide film can partially self-heal by in situ oxidation.
The film changes corrosion from direct metal dissolution to a process limited by ion penetration.
Relative to lower-temperature samples, the 1000 °C-treated alloy will have lower corrosion current density.
Relative to lower-temperature samples, the 1000 °C-treated alloy will have higher charge-transfer resistance.
The oxide-bearing alloy will exhibit reduced wear volume during combined wear-corrosion testing.
The oxide-bearing alloy will exhibit a lower coefficient of friction during combined wear-corrosion testing.
The improvement under combined degradation will be additive or synergistic relative to separate wear and corrosion tests.
Alloys sintered at 850–950 °C lack the robust, continuous oxide film present after treatment near 1000 °C.
The prediction holds when temperature supports oxide self-healing and mechanical stress does not immediately fracture the film.
The prediction may fail under extreme mechanical loads because the film is rapidly removed.
The prediction may fail at very low temperatures because oxidation kinetics become too slow to maintain the film.
A controlled test can compare samples sintered near 1000 °C with samples sintered at 850–950 °C during sliding in 3.5 wt% NaCl.
